title: After the White House
intro: Most former presidents write memoirs. Roosevelt shot big game in Africa, split his own party, took a bullet in the chest and gave the speech anyway, then nearly died mapping an unknown river in the Amazon. Fifteen questions on the busiest retirement in American history.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt do almost immediately after leaving office in 1909?
options: Went home to Sagamore Hill to write his memoirs
Took a professorship in history at Harvard
Ran for the Senate seat from New York
Left for a year-long expedition in Africa
questions.explanation: Taft was inaugurated on 4 March 1909 and Roosevelt sailed for East Africa on the 23rd, on an expedition backed by the Smithsonian. Part hunting trip, part scientific collecting expedition, it kept him out of his successor's way for the better part of a year — which was partly the point, since a former president loose in the country would have been read as a rival government. The Autobiography came later, in 1913, and he never took a chair at Harvard or ran for the Senate. He was fifty years old and had been president for seven and a half of them.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt and members of the safari party with a lion
questions.credit: Round the lion. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which institution sponsored the African expedition and received its specimens?
questions.explanation: The Smithsonian, with the American Museum of Natural History also involved. The expedition collected many thousands of specimens — birds, mammals, reptiles and plants — and much of it took years to catalogue. Roosevelt insisted the collecting was the purpose and the shooting merely the method.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt and others measuring a rhinoceros horn
questions.credit: Putting the tape on the rhino's horn. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Who accompanied Roosevelt on the African expedition as a fellow collector?
questions.explanation: Kermit, then nineteen and just finishing his first year at Harvard. He was the family's natural adventurer, and he would go with his father again to South America four years later — where he probably saved his life.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and Carl Akeley with an elephant
questions.credit: Father, Akeley, and elephant. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Why did Roosevelt break with his successor, William Howard Taft?
options: Taft's veto of the Payne–Aldrich tariff
Taft's decision to recognise the Chinese republic
Taft's drift to the party's conservative wing
A personal quarrel over royalties from his African book
questions.explanation: Roosevelt came home from Africa to find his hand-picked successor governing with the party's old guard rather than against it. The specifics were conservation and the trusts: Taft's Interior Secretary, Richard Ballinger, undid some of the land withdrawals, Gifford Pinchot went public about it and was fired for insubordination, and then Taft's Justice Department brought an antitrust suit against U.S. Steel that named Roosevelt's own 1907 decision as the wrong done. Taft also signed the Payne–Aldrich tariff instead of fighting it, which cost him the progressives. What began as policy disagreement turned personal and stayed that way for years; the two men did not speak again until 1918.
questions.imageAlt: Cartoon of the race to the White House with Wilson on a donkey and Taft on an elephant
questions.credit: Race to the White House, with Wilson on a donkey and Taft on an elephant. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's new party held its founding convention at Chicago in August 1912. What made it sound unlike other party conventions?
options: It refused to seat any delegate who had ever held office
The delegates sang hymns, and paraded round the hall singing them
The platform was written on the floor, by open vote
It adjourned twice for want of a quorum
questions.explanation: They sang “Onward, Christian Soldiers” and “The Battle Hymn of the Republic”, and marched through the hall doing it. Doris Kearns Goodwin, Kathleen Dalton and Lewis Gould all describe the same scene, and the comparison every one of them reaches for is a revival meeting. The delegates had come to found a cause as much as to nominate a candidate, and they behaved accordingly.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt standing beside his running mate after the 1912 nomination
questions.credit: Roosevelt and Johnson after nomination. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In October 1912, campaigning in Milwaukee, what happened to Roosevelt?
options: His campaign train derailed outside Racine
He was shot and spoke anyway
He collapsed from exhaustion and was ordered to bed
He lost his voice and finished the tour in silence
questions.explanation: A saloonkeeper named John Schrank shot him in the chest at close range as he stood in an open car outside the Gilpatrick Hotel. The bullet passed through the folded fifty-page speech in his breast pocket and his steel spectacle case before entering him. Reasoning that he was not coughing blood and so the lung was untouched, he insisted on being driven to the auditorium, opened by telling the crowd it took more than that to kill a bull moose, and spoke for the better part of an hour with the manuscript bloodied in his hand before he would go to hospital. Schrank was found insane and spent the rest of his life in a state institution.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt with Rough Rider veterans during the Bull Moose campaign in Chicago
questions.credit: T.R. with Rough Rider veterans during the Bull Moose campaign, Chicago. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

options: It lodged in the speech manuscript and never entered him
It was removed the same night
It stayed in his chest for the rest of his life
questions.explanation: Surgeons judged it more dangerous to dig it out than to leave it, and he carried it in his chest wall until he died seven years later.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and Hiram Johnson after the nomination
questions.credit: Roosevelt and Johnson after nomination. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: How did the 1912 presidential election end?
options: Woodrow Wilson won, with Roosevelt second and Taft third
The election went to the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: Roosevelt and Taft split the Republican vote and handed the presidency to Woodrow Wilson. Roosevelt finished second — still the strongest third-party showing in American history — and Taft, the sitting president, carried two states.
questions.imageAlt: Cartoon of the 1912 race to the White House
questions.credit: Race to the White House, with Wilson on a donkey and Taft on an elephant. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In 1913–14 Roosevelt joined an expedition to map an uncharted river. Where?
questions.explanation: The Rio da Dúvida — the River of Doubt — in the Brazilian Amazon, co-led with the Brazilian explorer Cândido Rondon. Nobody knew where it went. Roosevelt was fifty-five and had just lost a presidential election.
questions.credit: Putting the tape on the rhino's horn. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What happened to Roosevelt on that river?
options: He was bitten by a bushmaster and treated in camp
He came through the descent without injury
He turned back early and waited at the headwaters
He gashed his leg and nearly died of infection
questions.explanation: He went into the water to help free two canoes pinned against the rocks and cut his leg open on one of them. The wound became infected, malarial fever followed, and an old abscess from a carriage accident years earlier had to be lanced in the jungle without proper anaesthetic. At his worst he urged the others to go on and leave him behind, and he is said to have carried a fatal dose of morphine for exactly that purpose. Kermit refused to go, which settled it, because his father knew the boy would not leave the body. He came out perhaps fifty pounds lighter and never fully recovered his health.
questions.credit: Round the lion. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What is that river called today?
questions.explanation: The Brazilian government renamed it Rio Roosevelt in his honour. Locally it is often still called the Rio Teodoro.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt on expedition with Carl Akeley
questions.credit: Father, Akeley, and elephant. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt ask to do when the United States entered the First World War in 1917?
options: Raise a volunteer division and take it to France
Tour the country selling war bonds
questions.explanation: He asked President Wilson for permission to raise a volunteer division and lead it to France, at fifty-eight and in poor health. Wilson refused. Roosevelt never forgave him, and all four of his sons went instead.
questions.credit: T.R. with Rough Rider veterans during the Bull Moose campaign, Chicago. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which of Roosevelt's sons was killed in the First World War?
questions.explanation: Quentin, the youngest, a pursuit pilot shot down behind German lines on 14 July 1918. He was twenty. All four sons served: Theodore Jr. and Archibald were both wounded in France, and Kermit went first with the British in Mesopotamia because he could not wait for the American army. The Germans buried Quentin with military honours where he fell, and photographs of the grave were circulated as propaganda. Those close to Roosevelt said he never recovered; he died six months later.
questions.credit: Race to the White House, with Wilson on a donkey and Taft on an elephant. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Where and when did Roosevelt die?
questions.explanation: In his sleep at Sagamore Hill, in the early hours of January 6, 1919, aged sixty. His son Archie cabled his brothers: the old lion is dead.
questions.credit: Putting the tape on the rhino's horn. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How many books did Roosevelt write across his life?
questions.explanation: Around thirty-five, plus thousands of articles and an estimated hundred thousand letters. Several came out of this last decade alone — the African book, the Autobiography, and the account of the Brazilian river.
questions.credit: Round the lion. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
